headline: Simple urine test catches 9 in 10 bladder cancers, easing NHS strain
meta_description: A new at-home urine test detects bladder cancer with 92% accuracy, potentially sparing thousands of patients from uncomfortable hospital procedures each year.
summary_short: Researchers in England and Scotland have developed a urine test that spots bladder cancer in 92% of cases, with over 99% accuracy when results are negative.
body:
A new at-home urine test has shown remarkable promise in detecting bladder cancer, identifying the disease in 92 percent of cases during a trial involving nearly 1,000 patients across seven hospitals in England and Scotland. When the test came back negative, patients had better than a 99 percent chance of being disease-free. Called Galeas and developed at the University of Birmingham with funding from Cancer Research UK, the test scans for more than 450 mutations across 23 genes associated with bladder cancer—genetic material that cancer cells naturally shed into urine as they grow.

The real breakthrough lies not in replacing diagnosis entirely, but in triaging patients smarter. The UK performs over 300,000 cystoscopies annually—uncomfortable procedures where a small camera is inserted into the bladder—creating significant waiting lists in many areas. Galeas could help clinicians determine who needs urgent examination and who can safely wait, freeing up precious clinical time and resources. The trial enrolled patients already referred for suspected bladder cancer investigation, and results were published in European Urology Oncology.

Researchers emphasize this is early progress. A larger trial comes next, and if successful, tens of thousands of patients yearly could avoid cystoscopies altogether. Michelle Mitchell from Cancer Research UK noted that while further research is essential, finding faster, less invasive diagnostic paths is vital when too many people currently wait longer than they should for answers. Bladder cancer most commonly affects men over 60, with blood in urine as the typical first warning sign.
quick_facts: Detects bladder cancer in 92% of cases; 99%+ accuracy when negative
Developed at University of Birmingham, licensed to Nonacus diagnostics
Trial of 1,000 patients across seven hospitals in England and Scotland
Could spare tens of thousands from invasive cystoscopy procedures yearly
